Nice to meet you too. Two weeks, someone said. How has it been?
Very good. Difficult at the beginning, but easy now.
What was the difficult part? For most people it is the money.
The numbers, yes! At the till I never understood the total.
Nobody does. I have lived here twelve years and I still say "sorry, how much?"
Really? That makes me feel better.
It should. And what did you like most — the museums, the shops?
The shops. I like buying clothes for my children — and I did it alone, the first time.
With two children and a language you are learning? That is quite something.
Thank you. Maybe we come back in December. And you? Do you live here?

People always ask me about the big moments abroad: the airport, the police, the hospital. But the truth is that the big moments are rare, and the ordinary day is what really changes. Let me tell you about one Tuesday. In the morning I read the sign at the museum and I saw it was closed, so we did not cross the city for nothing. At eleven I called and booked for Wednesday instead, and I understood the last entry time. At lunch I ordered for four people and I asked about the nuts, because my son is allergic. In the afternoon I bought a coat for my daughter, in another colour, because the first one was not in her size and I asked. At the till I did not understand the total, so I asked the man to write it down, and he did, and nobody looked at me. And in the evening I sat on a bench for twenty minutes with another mother, and we talked about nothing at all. Not one emergency. That was the day everything changed.

After twenty lessons, students always ask me the same question: am I better, or am I the same? And it is a fair question, because progress at this level is invisible from the inside. So I tell them to stop measuring the wrong thing. Do not count the words you know. Count the situations you no longer avoid. At the start, most of my students avoid the shop, the telephone and the conversation with no purpose. Those three are the real map. If today you go into a shop alone, if you can call somebody and book a table, and if you can sit next to a stranger for ten minutes without looking at your phone, then you are not the same person who started, even if your grammar is exactly as it was. And one more thing, and please believe me on this: the ones who ask people to repeat learn faster than the ones who pretend to understand. Always.
